analysis.title: Can AI Be Both Power-Starved And Oversupplied? Goldman's Privorotsky Picks His Bear Case As Hedge Fund Nets Hit 5-Year Lows
key_insights: Goldman's Privorotsky says last week brought extraordinary de-risking. US fundamental long/short funds cut gross leverage the most in a week since Covid and cut net the most since Liberation Day (April 2025).

Privorotsky attributes the sell-off to AI spending: almost everything linked to AI spending was sold. The post-midterm rally lasted 24 hours, because the market cannot be this pessimistic on AI spending and this optimistic on the broader economy at once.

Put volume hit a record. More than 11mm puts traded in a single day (11.2 million contracts versus the prior record of 10.22 million on April 4, 2025). Index puts led, and single-stock put activity was the 4th highest day ever.

GS Prime data for US fundamental L/S funds: gross leverage fell 8.7 points in a week to 207.5%, net fell 3.7 points to 43.3%, and beta-adjusted gross fell 15.7 points. Net leverage is in the 1st percentile on one- and three-year lookbacks and the 0th percentile over five years.

The sell-off was mechanical as well as discretionary. SPX moved outside its recent range, gamma support disappeared, CTA selling accelerated, and double-digit semiconductor declines compounded the deleveraging.
Privorotsky's models suggest another ~$25bn+ of SPX CTA supply this week, on top of a ~$165 billion mechanical sell-off the prior week that Nomura's McElligott acknowledged he had underestimated.

Privorotsky does not accept the long-term bear argument that power constraints, permits and political delays undermine the AI buildout. If demand is real, capacity migrates to other states, countries or alternative power sources. He cites Mississippi, which is defending xAI's 2GW Southaven buildout and has over $25 billion in AWS commitments.

Privorotsky's bear case is oversupply. GPU spot rental rates remain supported by scarcity, but optimization and smaller specialized models are compressing per-token inference costs, so efficiency gains could outpace demand growth.

In Asia on Monday, semis bounced (TSMC +4.6%, MediaTek +9.8%, Tokyo Electron +2.7%, Taiex +4.9%, Nikkei +2.3%), but the rebound faded through the session. Taiwan tightened short selling rules and set up an NT$500bn stabilization fund.

Privorotsky says NDX futures would probably be considerably higher without the weekend Nvidia/Jensen Huang headlines (an alleged affair with a Chinese spy and a board probe). He reads it as idiosyncratic rather than a broader AI read-through, though it could affect sentiment.
CoreWeave (Tuesday) and Nebius (Thursday) earnings matter more for underlying AI sentiment, according to Privorotsky.

On defense, prediction markets give 10-15% odds of a year-end Ukraine ceasefire ahead of Abu Dhabi talks on November 10-11. Privorotsky's base case is a prolonged conflict. European defense multiples have compressed on ceasefire headlines and EU fiscal debates, while NATO 2%+ of GDP commitments and multi-year order backlogs mean a lot of bad news is priced in.

Oil is lower to start the week on no weekend escalation on Iran, after hedge funds sold $6.6 billion of Brent last week. Privorotsky expects an escalation premium to return to oil by Wednesday/Thursday absent diplomatic progress.

Privorotsky says semis look painfully oversold and would move up the quality curve first, such as ASML and TSMC. Whether to buy or sell the Friday bounce depends on incoming evidence on demand and monetization.
The macro backdrop has improved (energy lower, rates retracing, credit spreads tightening). Nasdaq has broken below its 200-day average, while the S&P's broader trend remains intact.
Friday payrolls were +165K (a 5-sigma beat), wages +0.4% MoM, unemployment 4.1%. Privorotsky says this adds pressure on the Fed. CPI on Tuesday is the main macro event this week.

Privorotsky's best-case outcome is range-bound trading, which lets implied volatility compress and systematic demand rebuild. With net leverage at five-year lows, the article notes a squeeze is possible and that Privorotsky's earlier year-end rally call is likely delayed rather than cancelled.

The author argues the oversupply thesis is a fundamental risk that range trading will not fix. $1.2 trillion of expected 2027 hyperscaler capex, much of it funded in the bond market, could be spent for a world of permanent scarcity if inference costs keep falling faster than demand grows.
